# Normal full-cover hinge stress outside finitely many cap budgets

This note proves normality of an attained cap-cover variational system at
all but finitely many interior feasible budgets, for a fixed finite family
of positive polytope fibers and a fixed cap count. The objective multiplier
is exactly one. Coverage contacts must be allowed to be finite measures
on primal-dual saddle pairs; a single factorized contact per fiber is not
claimed. No inequality giving the OC budget is deduced.

## 1. Definitions and theorem

Let `n>=0,d>=1`, let `P subset Z^n` be finite and nonempty, and let each
`K_z subset R^d` be a full-dimensional compact polytope. Define

`S=union_(z in P) ({z} x K_z)`,
`mu=sum_(z in P) vol_d|K_z`, `M=mu(S)>0`.

Fix a positive integer `N`. Parameters are

`p=((a_i,u_i,b_i))_(i=1)^N`, `a_i in R^n`, `|u_i|=1`, `b_i in R`,
`L_i(z,x)=a_i dot z+u_i dot x-b_i`, `H_i={L_i>=0}`.

Write

`c_i(p)=mu(S intersect H_i)`,
`Psi_i(p)=integral_S (L_i)_+ dmu`, `Psi=sum_i Psi_i`,
`s(p)=max_i c_i(p)/M`,
`F_z(p)=min_(x in K_z) max_i L_i(z,x)`.

Thus all the actual fibers are covered precisely when every `F_z>=0`.
In particular, their boundary points are included. The normals `a_i`
are unrestricted, so arbitrary oblique ambient halfspaces are retained.

Let `J` be the set of budgets `tau in (0,1)` for which some such cover
has `s(p)<=tau`. For `tau in J` put

`v(tau)=min {Psi(p): F_z(p)>=0 for every z, s(p)<=tau}`.       (1)

**Theorem.** The minimum in (1) is attained. The set `J` is an interval
with possibly missing endpoints. There is a finite set
`E subset int(J)` such that, for every `tau in int(J)\E`, **every**
minimizer of (1) has the normal stress in Section 6 below, with objective
multiplier one. All its coverage contacts belong to `S`; its section
terms use consistent coarea densities, including supporting-facet limits.

Consequently, if a cover with budget strictly below a given number
`alpha in (0,1)` exists, there is a budget between that cover's maximum
cap ratio and `alpha` with an attained normal hinge stress. This is a
conditional normality conclusion, not a proof that such a low-budget
cover cannot exist.

## 2. Attainment, local regularity, and semialgebraicity

Attainment is proved in Section 1 of
the full-cover hinge note (candidate de8d1a3251731edd).
Here are its essential steps, to fix its applicability. A bounded hinge
sequence bounds every fiber threshold `b_i-a_i dot z` below. After a
subsequence each threshold has a finite limit or tends to positive
infinity, while every `u_i` converges to a unit vector. The finite
thresholds lie in the restriction of the finite-dimensional space of
affine functions on `P`. Subtract a bounded right inverse of their
convergent errors from the sequence. One sufficiently late remaining
kernel vector is positive at all infinite-threshold coordinates and zero
at the finite ones. Scaling it realizes the exact finite limits and
thresholds above every fiber on all the other coordinates. This uses
finite coefficients, preserves every finite trace, and makes the other
caps empty. Hinges and cap masses then converge, since a nonvertical
hyperplane has zero `d`-volume in each fiber. Pointwise coverage passes
by the finite pigeonhole principle. This proves the claimed attainment
for the present polytopes, and equally for `n=0`.

All the following functions are locally Lipschitz on the parameter
manifold `X=(R^n x S^(d-1) x R)^N`:

`Psi_i`, `c_i`, `F_z`, `s`, and `G=max(0,max_z(-F_z))`.         (2)

For `F_z`, this follows by bounding the change of every `L_i` uniformly
on the compact fiber before taking a maximum and minimum. For `c_i`,
on a bounded parameter neighborhood with `|u_i|>=1/2`, a change of size
`epsilon` changes cap membership only in a slab of thickness
`O(epsilon)`. The volume of such a slab is at most its thickness times
a uniform bound for the `(d-1)`-dimensional projection volume of the
bounded fiber. For `d=1`, that projection volume is one. Finite summation
gives the assertion. The same bounds apply in a neighborhood in the
ambient parameter space.

The hinge is continuously differentiable there. Set

`Z_i=integral_(S intersect H_i) z dmu`,
`X_i=integral_(S intersect H_i) x dmu`.

Dominated differentiation of the positive part gives

`D Psi_i(dot p)=Z_i dot dot a_i+X_i dot dot u_i-c_i dot b_i`.   (3)

Continuity of these coefficients follows by dominated convergence,
because each limiting cap boundary has zero `mu`-mass.

For the fixed polytope data, all the functions in (2) are semialgebraic.
One should not justify this by a claim that arbitrary semialgebraic
integrals remain semialgebraic. Instead, intersect a fiber's finite
halfspace presentation with one extra cap inequality. Each possible
intersection vertex is obtained by solving a finite square linear
system; on its nonzero-determinant locus its coordinates are rational
functions of the cap coefficients. There are finitely many candidates.
Partition parameter space according to their determinant and feasibility
signs, incidences, and the signs needed for a fixed pulling triangulation.
On each of the finitely many resulting pieces, the clipped polytope's
volume and first moments are finite rational expressions obtained from
simplex determinants. Lower-dimensional clipped polytopes have zero
volume. Thus `c_i`, its first moments, and
`Psi_i=u_i dot X_i+a_i dot Z_i-b_i c_i` are semialgebraic.
The same conclusion for `F_z` follows either from its finite linear
program or directly from quantification over `K_z` and a real value.

The graph of `v` is consequently semialgebraic: express that a feasible
parameter has hinge `q`, and that no feasible parameter has hinge below
`q`, using finite first-order real quantifiers. Attainment makes this
the actual graph of (1). Projection/quantifier closure of semialgebraic
sets is the Tarski-Seidenberg theorem. A one-variable semialgebraic
function is `C^1` on the open intervals of some finite partition of its
domain, and hence is locally Lipschitz there. For these standard facts,
see Michel Coste's author-provided
[Introduction to O-minimal Geometry](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/228392940_An_introduction_to_O-minimal_geometry),
Theorems 1.13 and 6.7. Applying them to `v` gives a finite exceptional
set `E` as in the theorem. Feasibility is upward closed in the budget,
so `J` is an interval. If `J` is empty or has empty interior, the
normality assertion is simply vacuous.

The value is nonincreasing on `J`, since enlarging the budget enlarges
the feasible set. In particular `v'(tau)<=0` at every regular budget.

## 3. An exact, unrestricted coverage repair

For arbitrary parameters on `X`, define `R(p)` by keeping all `a_i,u_i`
and replacing every offset by

`b_i^R=b_i-G(p)`.

Every cap margin increases by the same constant `G(p)`, so

`F_z(R(p))=F_z(p)+G(p)>=0`,
`|R(p)-p|=sqrt(N) G(p)`.                                    (4)

The Euclidean distance here is the ambient product distance. In
particular, the repair stays on `X`, and it works simultaneously for
all whole fibers. It does not claim to preserve the cap budgets.

## 4. Two exact penalties and a normalized objective

Fix `tau in int(J)\E`, and let `p_*` be any minimizer at this budget.
Choose a finite local Lipschitz constant `A` for `v` near `tau`. For a
nearby **cover** `p`, if `s(p)<=tau` then `Psi(p)>=v(tau)`. If
`s(p)>tau`, then the cover itself proves that `s(p)` is feasible and

`Psi(p)>=v(s(p))>=v(tau)-A(s(p)-tau)`.

Thus `p_*` minimizes, locally among all covers,

`f(p)=Psi(p)+A(s(p)-tau)_+`.                                 (5)

This proof does not assume that the minimizing cover has a strictly
slack budget. If `s(p_*)<tau`, the same conclusion holds in a smaller
neighborhood, where the additional term is zero.

Let `B` be a local Lipschitz constant for `f` near `p_*`. By (4), for
every sufficiently close `p in X`, the repaired cover is still in that
neighborhood and

`f(p)>=f(R(p))-B sqrt(N)G(p)>=f(p_*)-B sqrt(N)G(p)`.

It follows that `p_*` is an unconstrained local minimizer on `X` of

`Phi(p)=Psi(p)+A(s(p)-tau)_+ + B sqrt(N)G(p)`.                (6)

The hinge coefficient is exactly one. Ordinary locally Lipschitz
Fermat and sum/maximum rules applied in smooth sphere charts yield
normal stationarity. More explicitly, a generalized gradient of a
maximum lies in the convex hull of generalized gradients of its active
arguments. The hinge has its single gradient (3). The budget term
contributes nonnegative multiples of gradients of caps with
`c_i=tau M`; the coverage term contributes nonnegative multiples of
`-F_z` for fibers with `F_z=0`. Restoring the sphere normals introduces
one real scalar multiplier per cap. The exact contact descriptions
needed to interpret these gradients are proved next.

For clarity, the locally Lipschitz generalized gradient used here is the
convex hull of limits of ordinary gradients at differentiability points.
Its Fermat rule follows by separating that compact convex set from
zero: strict separation gives a direction with uniformly negative
nearby directional upper bound, contradicting local minimality.
The sum and maximum inclusions follow by taking differentiability
sequences and convexifying. These are inclusions, which suffice for
the existence of the multipliers below; equality rules are unnecessary.

### Exact total budget sensitivity

There is a stronger choice of penalty which will fix the sum of the
budget multipliers exactly. Suppose first that `s(p_*)=tau`. Since
`v` is `C^1` on a neighborhood of `tau`, the function

`f_0(p)=Psi(p)-v(s(p))`                                      (6a)

is well-defined and locally Lipschitz near `p_*`. On every nearby
cover it is nonnegative, by the definition of `v`, and it vanishes
at `p_*`. Applying the coverage repair (4) again makes

`f_0(p)+B_0 sqrt(N)G(p)`

an unconstrained local minimum on `X`, where `B_0` is a local
Lipschitz constant of `f_0`. The chain and maximum rules express the
budget term as

`-v'(tau) sum_i omega_i D c_i/M`,
`omega_i>=0`, `sum_i omega_i=1`,
`omega_i>0 => c_i=tau M`.

Each selected `D c_i` belongs to its consistent generalized-gradient
set. Consequently the resulting multipliers can be chosen with

`M sum_i r_i=-v'(tau)`.                                     (6b)

This remains valid when `v'(tau)=0`, with all `r_i=0`.

If instead `s(p_*)<tau`, the same `p_*` is feasible at every budget
between `s(p_*)` and `tau`. Monotonicity and minimality therefore make
`v` constant on that interval, so differentiability at `tau` gives
`v'(tau)=0`. In a sufficiently small neighborhood of `p_*`, every
cover already obeys the budget. Thus `Psi` itself has a local minimum
among covers; applying (4) directly yields the normal stress with
`r_i=0`, again proving (6b).

The identity (6b) uses the actual attained value function, rather than
an unproved uniform bound on cap-section multipliers. It is a sensitivity
identity only; its right-hand side can be large.

## 5. Consistent section gradients and finite saddle-contact measures

For a cap, put `T_iz=K_z intersect {L_i(z,x)=0}`. Every generalized
cap-mass gradient has the form

`(Z_i^s,X_i^s,-S_i)`,                                       (7)

where a single consistent section measure `tau_i` supplies all entries:

`d tau_i(z,x)=theta_iz(x) dH_(d-1)(x)/|u_i|` on `T_iz`,
`0<=theta_iz<=1`,
`S_i=int d tau_i`, `Z_i^s=int z d tau_i`, `X_i^s=int x d tau_i`.

Here `|u_i|=1`; the denominator records the coarea convention. On a
proper section through the fiber interior, `theta_iz=1` almost
everywhere. At a coincident supporting facet it can be a measurable
function of the facet point. Its different moments cannot be chosen
independently. To see (7), take regular nearby sections, project them
onto the limiting cap plane, and take weak limits. Projection Jacobians
tend to one and the projected indicator densities lie in `[0,1]`.
Interior section points are eventually present. Convex combinations
retain domination and the same moments. This also covers `d=1`, with
point masses in `[0,1]` at endpoints. In particular, all chosen section
data satisfy

`u_i dot X_i^s+a_i dot Z_i^s-b_i S_i=0`.                     (8)

For a fiber, finite convex minimax gives

`F_z=max_(lambda in Delta_N) min_(x in K_z)
           sum_i lambda_i L_i(z,x)`.                         (9)

Both extrema attain. A primal-dual saddle pair consists of a minimizer
`x` of `max_i L_i` and a maximizing `lambda` in (9). Its features are

`g_z(x,lambda)_(a_i,u_i,b_i)=lambda_i(z,x,-1)`.                (10)

The generalized gradient of `F_z` is contained in the convex hull of
these features at actual saddle pairs. Here is a finite-polytope proof.
Write the primal as the linear program minimizing `s` subject to
`x in K_z` and `L_i(z,x)<=s`. On each of finitely many open parameter
cells, optimal nonsingular primal and dual bases can be chosen fixed;
their solutions are rational functions of the parameters. Restrict
further if necessary to a full-dimensional cell on which those rational
functions are differentiable. Differentiating the value there gives
(10): multiply the differentiated active cap equalities by their dual
weights; the terms from `dot x` cancel against the fixed fiber-facet
dual equations, and the weights sum to one. This is also a direct
differentiation of the primal-dual Lagrangian. Such cells exhaust a
dense open set. At their limiting points the primal points remain in
compact `K_z` and the weights in compact `Delta_N`; any limit is still
a saddle pair by continuity of the margins and of `F_z`. The definition
of generalized gradient now proves the inclusion. Degenerate optimal
faces cause no problem: an optimal basic solution can be selected on
the neighboring full-dimensional cells. Since all fibers are bounded,
the primal optimum has a vertex; dual cap weights can likewise be
chosen within the compact simplex.

Therefore a chosen generalized coverage gradient can be written using
a finite probability measure `nu_z` on saddle pairs. Finiteness follows
from finite-dimensional Caratheodory after taking the compact feature
image. Define

`p_zi=int lambda_i d nu_z(x,lambda)`,
`q_zi=int lambda_i x d nu_z(x,lambda)`.

Then its cap `i` block is `(z p_zi,q_zi,-p_zi)`. In general there is no
single point `x_z` with `q_zi=p_zi x_z` for all `i`, and this proof
does not make that assertion.

At an active coverage constraint, `F_z=0`. For every saddle pair in
this finite representation,

`L_i(z,x)<=0` for every `i`,
`lambda_i L_i(z,x)=0` for every `i`,
`-sum_i lambda_i u_i in N_Kz(x)`.                            (11)

Indeed the primal maximum is zero, its weighted average is the dual
value zero, and `x` minimizes that weighted affine function. Thus all
selected points `(z,x)` belong to the actual set `S`, and each
positively assigned cap meets its assigned point on the boundary.

## 6. The normal cap/section/contact equations

Applying the stationarity of (6) with Sections 3--5 gives finite
nonnegative numbers `r_i,eta_z`, consistent section data (7), finite
probability measures `nu_z` as above for active fibers, and real sphere
multipliers `sigma_i`, such that

`r_i(c_i-tau M)=0`, `eta_z F_z=0`,                            (12)

`c_i+r_i S_i = sum_z eta_z p_zi`,                            (13)

`Z_i+r_i Z_i^s = sum_z eta_z z p_zi`,                        (14)

`X_i+r_i X_i^s-sum_z eta_z q_zi+sigma_i u_i=0`.              (15)

The objective multiplier is one. Using (6a) instead of (5), the
multipliers can moreover be chosen to satisfy the exact identity

`M sum_i r_i=-v'(tau)`.                                     (12a)

The coverage multipliers have a finite local bound
`sum_z eta_z<=B_0 sqrt(N)` from that coverage penalty (or from the
direct hinge penalty in the slack-budget case). These are sensitivity
statements, not universal dimension bounds. Empty inactive
fiber measures may be assigned arbitrarily because their multipliers
are zero.

There is an exact per-cap Euler cancellation. Subtract `b_i` times
(13) from the sum of the inner products of (14) with `a_i` and (15)
with `u_i`. The cap term is `Psi_i`; the section term is zero by (8);
each contact term is zero by (11). Since `|u_i|=1`, the result is

`sigma_i=-Psi_i`.

Equivalently,

`X_i+r_i X_i^s
       =sum_z eta_z q_zi+Psi_i u_i`.                         (16)

In measure terms, the cap-and-section measure
`mu|H_i+r_i tau_i` and the contact measure

`sum_z eta_z integral lambda_i delta_(z,x) d nu_z(x,lambda)`

have the same total mass and the same real integer-base first moment.
Their continuous first moments differ by exactly `Psi_i u_i`. All
supporting-fiber forces in (11) remain in this statement. No convex-order
comparison between these measures is asserted.

## 7. Scope and consequences for the ongoing variational route

The exceptional set is finite for each fixed polytope family and cap
count. It is independent of which minimizer at a regular budget is
chosen. The proof allows cap/facet coincidences, flat cap-volume
profiles, nonunique coverage minimizers, and unbounded integer tilt
parameters across minimizing sequences. Its local stress is realized
with finite parameters and actual contacts after the attainment step.

The proof does not apply semialgebraic regularity to arbitrary curved
fibers, does not vary the body, and does not establish normality at the
minimum feasible budget. In particular it is consistent with the
nonregular simplex-product abnormality at its exact sharp budget in
the earlier obstruction (candidate 2a5e48e3badc4c86).

If a strict low-budget cover of a fixed polytope family exists, the open
interval above its cap maximum contains regular budgets, so abnormality
can be avoided for an attained hinge minimizer in that interval. The
remaining task would be a quantitative inequality using (13)--(16) and
the actual small cap budget. No such inequality is supplied here, and
the already disproved universal per-group or convex-order assertions
are not reinstated by this normality theorem.
